What I found:
- The Riemann hypothesis is still open. The Clay Mathematics Institute still lists it as an unsolved Millennium Prize Problem, and every source checked (Clay, Wikipedia, Quanta, Science News) treats it as unproven. A claimed proof from MIT in 2019 would have been major news, and I found no trace of one.
- My search for the paper itself was incomplete. Most arXiv queries were rate-limited (HTTP 429). One broad arXiv query for "Smith Chen Riemann" returned no results, but it was not restricted by author or date. Google Scholar and MIT's own repositories were never actually searched. So I can't rule out a paper with a similar description, but I found no evidence that one exists.
- The closest real 2019 work is not by Smith and Chen and does not prove the hypothesis. Griffin, Ono, Rolen and Zagier published a paper in PNAS in May 2019 on Jensen polynomials and the Riemann zeta function. They proved a significant partial result (many of the Jensen polynomials have only real roots) and say explicitly that it falls short of a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. None of those authors is at MIT.
- The notable MIT-linked result is from 2024, by Larry Guth (MIT) and James Maynard (Oxford). It improves bounds on how many zeta zeros can lie off the critical line (a zero-density estimate). It is also a partial result, not a proof.
